claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline is a single-phase FCC alloy.
Cold rolling followed by rapid annealing can produce the baseline and modified alloys with similar initial dislocation densities.
Removing Ni from equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni yields equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co.
Removing Ni from equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni reduces the stacking fault energy.
Removing Ni reduces local chemical complexity in the alloy.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi has an intermediate stacking fault energy of approximately 25-30 mJ/m2.
The intermediate stacking fault energy of CoCrFeMnNi permits both dislocation slip and mechanical twinning during plastic deformation.
Stacking fault energy governs whether FCC alloys deform primarily by perfect-dislocation slip, mechanical twinning, or strain-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation.

High stacking fault energy above about 45 mJ/m2 favors perfect-dislocation slip, intermediate energy of 15-45 mJ/m2 favors twinning, and low energy below about 15 mJ/m2 favors FCC-to-HCP martensitic transformation.
The proposed Ni-removal-induced change in stacking fault energy alters dislocation nucleation, motion, cross-slip, and twinning activity.
Changes in dislocation and twinning activity alter strain hardening and incipient plasticity.
Mechanical twinning and martensitic transformation can improve strength and ductility.
The Ni-free Cr-Mn-Fe-Co alloy should exhibit altered incipient plasticity relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
The Ni-free alloy should have a measurably different strength-ductility balance from the quinary baseline, although the direction of the change is not predicted.
Nanoindentation responses can reveal differences in incipient plasticity and can depend on alloy microstructure.
High-resolution TEM and X-ray diffraction can quantitatively determine or infer stacking fault energy in these alloys.
Intrinsic chemical variation can promote three-dimensional stacking-fault networks and associated FCC-to-HCP transformation in dual-phase HEAs.
The hypothesis is limited to single-phase FCC alloys with comparable processing, grain structure, and initial dislocation density.
Additional phases or substantially different processing routes can introduce deformation mechanisms that invalidate the proposed comparison.
